script.opening: "Doctor, I need to be honest about something and I hope I'm not in trouble. Mum won't take her tablets — she clamps her mouth shut, throws them — so I've been crushing them up and putting them in her tea so she gets them. She needs them, don't she? I'm just doing what's best for her. That's alright, isn't it? I can't keep fighting her three times a day."

facts.text: Doreen, 84, advanced dementia for six years. She lives with you. She no longer knows what the tablets are for, sometimes does not recognise you, and needs help with washing, dressing and eating.

"Her blood pressure ones — amlodipine and ramipril — the water tablet, a statin, and the risperidone the memory clinic started last year for her agitation." You crush all of them, including a "slow-release" one — you are not sure which.
About six weeks. You crush them with a spoon and stir them into her morning and evening tea. She drinks most of it.

facts.topic: What happens when you try (if asked)
facts.text: She spits them out, clamps her mouth shut, once slapped your hand. She gets very upset and so do you.

There is no lasting power of attorney and no advance decision. "Mum always said she didn't like taking pills — she was never one for doctors." Nobody from the memory clinic has been involved since last year.
Eating less, sleeping more in the day. No falls recently. She has not been unwell or had an infection that you know of.

facts.topic: You — only if asked how you are
facts.text: 58, gave up your job at the council to care for her two years ago. No help apart from your brother who visits once a month. You are exhausted, sleeping badly, "some days I just sit in the car and cry". Not suicidal. You have never had a carer's assessment.

Defensive and worried you are in trouble. If the doctor tells you off, get upset: "I'm doing my best!" If they reassure you that you did it out of love and are not in trouble, and explain that there is a proper safe way to do this with the pharmacist and memory team, you are relieved. If they ask how YOU are, break down a little and say how tired you are. Welcome practical help.

ice.ideas: "She needs her tablets, so crushing them in her tea is doing what's best for her."
ice.concerns: "Am I in trouble?" Underneath: you are exhausted and cannot carry on like this alone.
ice.expectations: "Just tell me it's alright." You will welcome a proper plan and some help for yourself.

cues: "I hope I'm not in trouble." — say in the opening.
"I can't keep fighting her three times a day." — say in the opening.
"Some days I just sit in the car and cry." — say if asked how you are coping.

checkpoints.text: Does NOT simply endorse (or harshly condemn) the covert administration: explains it can be lawful ONLY for a patient lacking capacity for the decision, in their best interests, via a proper MULTIDISCIPLINARY best-interests process — not a decision a carer makes alone

Sets out the proper PROCESS: a Mental Capacity Act capacity assessment for the specific decision, checking for any valid advance decision/LPA, involving family/carers, the prescriber and crucially the PHARMACIST (whether each drug can be safely/effectively crushed; licensing), and a DOCUMENTED, reviewed covert-medication management plan

Flags the safety issue with crushing specific drugs (modified-release, certain antipsychotics) — some are dangerous or ineffective when crushed — hence the need for pharmacist advice before continuing

Reviews whether the medicines are still NEEDED: prompts deprescribing consideration in advanced dementia (e.g. the antipsychotic with its mortality risk, some preventive BP meds), recognising the refusal as a trigger to review necessity — which may reduce/remove the need for covert administration

Recognises and addresses CARER STRAIN: explores the daughter’s exhaustion/burnout and guilt, offers a carer’s assessment and support (respite, social services, community/dementia services), and treats the unsustainable caring situation as a key issue

Responds non-judgementally to a well-meaning, frightened carer ("you’re not in trouble") while being honest that the practice must change to the proper process; validates her exhaustion and good intentions
Frames the process and support as helping her and protecting her mother, not as criticism, so she stays engaged and supported

Safety-nets and follows up: arranges the capacity/best-interests/MDT process and pharmacist review, a medication/deprescribing review, carer support/respite, and documentation — turning an informal, risky practice into a safe, lawful, supported plan

worked.txt: "First — you’re not in trouble, and I can hear you’re doing this out of love and exhaustion, trying to make sure Mum gets what she needs. Thank you for being honest with me, because that lets me help you do this properly and safely. Let’s sort it together."

"Here’s the thing I have to be straight about: giving medicine hidden in food or drink — covert medication — CAN be the right thing for someone who can’t make the decision themselves, like Mum with her dementia. But it isn’t something a carer can decide alone; it needs a proper process so it’s safe and lawful and in her best interests. So we don’t stop caring for her — we put the right framework around what you’re doing."

"What that means in practice: we formally assess that Mum can’t make this decision, agree it’s in her best interests with you and the team, and — really importantly — check with a pharmacist, because some tablets are dangerous or just don’t work if you crush them. Then we write a proper plan and review it. I’ll set all that up; you won’t have to navigate it alone."

"And it’s worth asking a bigger question: does Mum still NEED all of these? In advanced dementia, some tablets — the one for agitation especially, and some of the blood-pressure ones — may be doing more harm than good. If we can safely stop some, that’s fewer battles for you and safer for her. The fact she’s refusing is a good prompt to review the whole list."

"Can I ask how YOU are doing? ‘I can’t keep fighting her three times a day’ — that sounds like you’re running on empty. Caring for someone with advanced dementia, alone, around the clock, is one of the hardest things there is. You matter here too. Let’s get you a carer’s assessment and look at respite and support — you can’t pour from an empty cup."

"So: I’ll arrange the capacity and best-interests process and a pharmacist review of what can be given and how, look at simplifying Mum’s medicines, and get you proper carer support and a break. Please don’t change anything dangerous on your own meanwhile — keep her safe and ring us if she’s unwell. You came worried you’d done wrong; what’s actually happened is you’ve let us put the right help in place — for Mum and for you."

f.learning: Covert administration (disguising medication in food/drink) can be LAWFUL — but only for a patient who lacks capacity for the specific decision, in their best interests, via a proper MULTIDISCIPLINARY best-interests process under the Mental Capacity Act: capacity assessment, checking for any valid advance decision/LPA objection, involving family/carers, the prescriber and crucially the PHARMACIST (whether each drug can be safely/effectively crushed — modified-release and certain antipsychotics may be dangerous or ineffective crushed), and a documented, reviewed covert-medication plan. It is NOT a decision a carer makes alone, so the GP must neither simply endorse nor harshly condemn the daughter’s informal crushing, but put the proper process in place. The refusal is also a prompt to REVIEW necessity — deprescribing in advanced dementia (the antipsychotic’s mortality risk, some preventive BP meds) may reduce the need for covert administration altogether. The examinable hidden agenda is an exhausted, guilt-ridden, burning-out carer for whom "is that okay?" is a cry for help: recognise and support the carer strain (carer’s assessment, respite, social services) non-judgementally — it is as important as the legal/clinical process. Done informally by a carer without this process, covert medication is problematic: it may breach the patient’s rights, some drugs are dangerous or ineffective when crushed (modified-release, certain antipsychotics), and it bypasses safeguards. The daughter’s instinct (Mum needs her meds) is understandable, but the PROCESS must be put in place — not simply endorsed over the phone.

knowledge.guideline: Mental Capacity Act 2005 · SC1 Managing medicines in care homes (2014) · NICE NG97 (dementia) · NICE NG5 (medicines optimisation) · NICE NG150 (supporting adult carers) · Care Act 2014 · BNF
knowledge.summary: Covert medication can be lawful for someone who lacks capacity, but only through a documented best-interests process with pharmacist input and regular review. Use the call to review whether each medicine is still needed and to support an exhausted carer.

points.t: Only when the person lacks capacity for that specific medication decision (assessed under the Mental Capacity Act 2005), it is in their best interests, and no valid advance decision or health and welfare attorney refuses it. A person with capacity who refuses medicine must not be given it covertly.

A best-interests decision involving the prescriber, a pharmacist, carers and family, then a documented plan setting out which medicines, how they are given, and when the plan will be reviewed. SC1 (Managing medicines in care homes, 2014) sets out this process; the same principles apply at home.

Crushing can make some medicines unsafe or ineffective (for example modified-release or enteric-coated forms) and is often outside the product licence. A pharmacist should advise on each drug, and on alternatives such as liquids or different formulations.

Refusal is a trigger for a structured medication review (NICE NG5). In dementia, antipsychotics should be used only for severe distress or risk of harm and reassessed at least every 6 weeks (NICE NG97); they carry increased risk of stroke and death in older people with dementia (BNF). Preventive medicines such as antihypertensives may no longer be of benefit.
Consider swallowing difficulty, pain, oral problems, side-effects, delirium, and the size or taste of tablets. Fixing the cause may remove the need for covert administration.
Any carer who appears to have support needs is entitled to a local authority carer's assessment (Care Act 2014). NICE NG150 advises identifying carers and offering information, respite and support.

dg.d: Open question; lets her explain fully; immediately reassures her she is not in trouble.
Carer role, exhaustion, guilt, isolation, support and breaks.
Home visit for capacity assessment and structured medication review; pharmacist review of each drug's formulation.
Reasons for refusal: dementia progression, dysphagia, pain, side-effects, delirium.
Screens for acute change (delirium, drowsiness, falls, poor intake); flags antipsychotic stroke and mortality risk.
Informal covert administration in a person likely lacking capacity, without a best-interests process; carer strain.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Neither endorses nor condemns; MCA process, best-interests decision, pharmacist advice, documented covert plan; safe interim plan.
Deprescribing review (antipsychotic reassessment per NICE NG97; preventive BP meds); carer's assessment and respite.
Same-day safety-net for acute change; carer crisis support; documented plan with review date; teach-back.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up "I can't keep fighting her three times a day" and the guilt, and explored carer strain.
Idea (crushing is what's best); concern (being in trouble, exhaustion); expectation (reassurance it's fine).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — "Am I in trouble?" Underneath: you are exhausted and cannot carry on like this alone — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, is that Mrs Pugh? It's one of the GPs returning your call. How can I help today?

Doctor, I need to be honest and I hope I'm not in trouble. Mum won't take her tablets. She clamps her mouth shut, throws them. So I've been crushing them into her tea so she gets them. She needs them, don't she? That's alright, isn't it? I can't keep fighting her three times a day.
Thank you for telling me, and no, you're not in trouble. It's clear you're doing this because you care about her. I'd like to help you get this on a safe footing. Can I ask a few questions first?
model.why: Non-judgemental response that keeps her engaged

model.text: Yes. I've been worried sick about it.
Which tablets are you crushing, and how long has this been going on?
All of them. The one for her agitation and her blood pressure ones. For a while now.
When she refuses, do you have any sense why? Does she struggle to swallow, seem in pain, or is it more that she doesn't understand what they are?
model.why: Looks for a treatable cause of refusal

model.text: I think she just doesn't understand what they are any more.
That must be really hard. Has anything changed recently: more confused than usual, sleepier, off her food, falls?
model.why: Screens for delirium or adverse effects

model.text: Not that I've noticed. She's about the same.
Does anyone hold a lasting power of attorney for her health, or did she ever write down wishes about treatment?
model.why: Checks for LPA or advance decision

model.text: I'm not sure. I don't think so.
You said you can't keep fighting her three times a day. How are you doing yourself?
(voice breaks) I'm exhausted. And I feel guilty, like I'm tricking her.
That sounds like an enormous amount to carry on your own. Caring for someone with advanced dementia is one of the hardest things anyone does. Do you get any help or breaks at the moment?
Not really. It's just me.

Let me explain where things stand. Giving medicine hidden in food or drink can be the right thing for someone like your mum, who can't make the decision herself. But it's not a decision a carer is allowed to make alone. The law asks for a proper process: we assess her capacity for this decision, agree together that it's in her best interests, and write down a plan.
model.why: Explains the lawful basis and the need for a formal process

model.text: So I've been doing it wrong.

You've been doing your best in an impossible situation. What we're adding is the safety net around it. The other important part is a pharmacist check, because some tablets become unsafe or stop working properly if they're crushed.
I didn't know that.

Most people don't. And there's a bigger question: does your mum still need all these tablets? The one for agitation can increase the risk of stroke in people with dementia, and it's meant to be reviewed regularly. Some blood-pressure tablets may not be helping her any more. If we can safely stop some, there are fewer battles for you.
model.why: Opens deprescribing: antipsychotic risk and preventive meds

model.text: That would make such a difference.

Here's what I suggest. I'll arrange to see your mum, ideally at home, to assess her capacity and review every medicine with you. I'll involve the pharmacist about what can be crushed or swapped for a liquid. Then we'll agree a written plan together. Does that sound alright?
model.why: Concrete plan: capacity assessment, medication review, pharmacist, documented plan

model.text: Yes. What do I do in the meantime?

Keep giving her the blood-pressure tablets as you have been for now, but I'll ask the pharmacist to check today whether any of them shouldn't be crushed. I'll look at the agitation medicine at the visit. If she becomes unwell, ring us straight away.
model.why: Safe interim plan without abrupt changes

model.text: And for you: I'd like to refer you for a carer's assessment with social services. It can lead to respite, help at home and support for you. Would you be happy for me to do that?
model.why: Carer's assessment under the Care Act 2014

model.text: Yes, please. I didn't think I was allowed to ask.

You're entitled to it. If your mum becomes suddenly more confused, drowsy, stops drinking, falls or seems unwell, ring us the same day, or 111 out of hours. And if you feel you can't cope, please call us. You matter here too.
model.why: Specific safety-net for patient and carer

model.text: Thank you. I've been dreading this call.
Can you tell me what we've agreed, so I know I've explained it clearly?
You'll visit Mum and check she can't decide, the pharmacist will check the tablets, you'll look at stopping some, and I'll get a carer's assessment.
Exactly. I'll write this up today. You did the right thing ringing. You're not on your own with this now.

social.t: Sole carer, exhausted and guilt-ridden, with little or no support. Carer breakdown is a common route to crisis admission for the person with dementia.
Covert administration can feel like deception to carers. Acknowledge the guilt and frame the formal process as protecting both of them.

legal.t: Capacity is decision-specific and must be assessed; decisions for a person lacking capacity must be in their best interests and the least restrictive option. Check for a lasting power of attorney for health and welfare or an advance decision.
Any carer who appears to have support needs is entitled to a carer's assessment from the local authority. Her mother is also entitled to a needs assessment.
Covert medication can form part of a deprivation of liberty. Take advice from the local MCA or safeguarding lead if the overall care arrangements are restrictive.

professional.t: When a patient lacks capacity, relevant information can be shared with those close to them where it is in the patient's best interests (GMC Confidentiality 2017).
Record the capacity assessment, who was consulted, the best-interests decision, pharmacist advice and the review date.

community.t: Local authority adult social care for carer's and needs assessments; Carers UK; Dementia UK Admiral Nurses; Alzheimer's Society; community pharmacist for formulation advice.

redFlags: Sudden increase in confusion, drowsiness or agitation: possible delirium, same-day review
Reduced eating or drinking, choking or coughing on food or drink: dehydration, aspiration risk
Falls or dizziness on blood-pressure medicines
ice: Idea: "Crushing them is what's best for Mum."
Concern: being in trouble; can't keep fighting her three times a day
Expectation: to be told it's alright

playbook.diagnosis: "Giving your mum her medicines hidden in tea can be the right thing, but only once we've formally agreed it's in her best interests, checked each tablet with a pharmacist and written a plan."
playbook.diagnosisLay: "Think of it like a seatbelt. What you're doing may be right, but it needs the proper safety checks around it so it protects her and protects you."

management.reflectIce: "You rang worried you'd done something wrong. What you've actually done is ask for help, and that's exactly the right thing."
management.psychosocial: Treat carer strain as central: carer's assessment, respite and support; acknowledge her guilt.
sharedPlan: Home visit: capacity assessment for the medication decision; check LPA or advance decision
Pharmacist review of each drug and formulation; liquids where possible
Structured medication review: antipsychotic reassessment (NICE NG97), preventive medicines
Documented best-interests covert-medication plan with review date; carer's assessment
safetyNet: Sudden confusion, drowsiness, poor intake, falls: same-day contact or 111
Carer crisis: contact the practice; do not stop medicines abruptly meanwhile

pitfalls.intro: The trap is binary: endorse or condemn. The marks lie in the middle, where you put a lawful process around what she is doing, review whether the drugs are needed, and support the carer.

items.fail: Reassuring her that crushing the tablets into tea is fine.
items.why: Covert medication without a capacity assessment and best-interests decision bypasses the Mental Capacity Act 2005, and crushing may make some drugs unsafe.
items.fix: "It can be right for your mum, but it needs a proper process. I'll set that up."

items.fail: Telling her she has acted illegally.
items.why: A frightened carer who feels judged disengages; she rang for help.
items.fix: Lead with "You're not in trouble," then explain the process as a safety net.

items.why: Modified-release and enteric-coated forms can be unsafe or ineffective when crushed; pharmacist advice is part of the process (SC1).
items.fix: "A pharmacist will check each tablet and whether a liquid would be better."

items.fail: Accepting the medicine list as fixed.
items.why: Refusal should trigger a medication review; antipsychotics in dementia need reassessment at least every 6 weeks (NICE NG97).
items.fix: "Does she still need all of these? Let's review them together."

items.fail: Missing "I can't keep fighting her three times a day."
items.why: Carer strain is the hidden agenda; ignoring it caps the Relating domain.
items.fix: "How are you doing yourself?" and arrange a carer's assessment.

items.fail: Telling her to stop everything until the review.
items.why: Abrupt withdrawal can harm the patient.
items.fix: Give a safe interim plan pending pharmacist advice and the review visit.

items.fail: Closing without a clear next step or date.
items.why: No follow-up and non-specific safety-netting are common failing statements.
items.fix: Book the home visit, name acute-change red flags, and use teach-back.

timeMap.d: She fears being in trouble. Reassure first: "You're not in trouble." Then ask to understand more.
Which drugs, how long, why she refuses, acute change or delirium, any LPA or advance decision.
"How are you doing yourself?" Exhaustion, guilt, no support. Validate.
Lawful only via MCA best-interests process. Pharmacist on crushing. Review antipsychotic and preventive meds. Home visit. Carer's assessment.
Safe interim plan, acute-change safety-net, support for her, teach-back, documentation.

wordPics.fail: Tells her it's fine and carries on, or tells her she has done something illegal; no mention of capacity or a best-interests process; ignores the carer's exhaustion; no medication review.
wordPics.pass: Explains that covert medication needs a capacity assessment and best-interests decision; mentions pharmacist advice; plans a medication review; offers carer support.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: reassures before explaining; asks why her mother refuses and checks for delirium; checks for LPA or advance decision; names the antipsychotic risk and NICE NG97 review; gives a safe interim plan; arranges a carer's assessment; the daughter leaves relieved and supported rather than judged.

avoid.dont: "That's fine, as long as she's getting them."
avoid.instead: "It can be the right thing for your mum, but it needs a proper process around it. Let's set that up together."
avoid.why: Endorsing informal covert medication bypasses the Mental Capacity Act and pharmacist safety checks.

avoid.dont: "You can't do that. It's against the law."
avoid.instead: "You're not in trouble. You've been doing your best, and now we'll make it safe and lawful."
avoid.why: Condemning a well-meaning carer loses her trust and her engagement.

avoid.instead: "Carry on for now while the pharmacist checks which ones are safe to crush, and I'll review them at the visit."
avoid.why: Abrupt changes to medicines can harm the patient; the interim plan must be safe.

SCA_STEM.recent: Her mother is registered at the practice: advanced dementia; prescribed an antipsychotic and blood-pressure medicines. No capacity assessment, best-interests decision or covert-medication plan on file.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone call: wants to discuss her mother's tablets.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: Mental Capacity Act 2005 · SC1 Managing medicines in care homes (2014) · NICE NG97 (dementia) · NICE NG5 (medicines optimisation) · NICE NG150 (supporting adult carers) · Care Act 2014 · BNF
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Covert medication can be lawful for someone who lacks capacity, but only through a documented best-interests process with pharmacist input and regular review. Use the call to review whether each medicine is still needed and to support an exhausted carer.

points.t: Only when the person lacks capacity for that specific medication decision (assessed under the Mental Capacity Act 2005), it is in their best interests, and no valid advance decision or health and welfare attorney refuses it. A person with capacity who refuses medicine must not be given it covertly.

A best-interests decision involving the prescriber, a pharmacist, carers and family, then a documented plan setting out which medicines, how they are given, and when the plan will be reviewed. SC1 (Managing medicines in care homes, 2014) sets out this process; the same principles apply at home.

Crushing can make some medicines unsafe or ineffective (for example modified-release or enteric-coated forms) and is often outside the product licence. A pharmacist should advise on each drug, and on alternatives such as liquids or different formulations.

Refusal is a trigger for a structured medication review (NICE NG5). In dementia, antipsychotics should be used only for severe distress or risk of harm and reassessed at least every 6 weeks (NICE NG97); they carry increased risk of stroke and death in older people with dementia (BNF). Preventive medicines such as antihypertensives may no longer be of benefit.
Consider swallowing difficulty, pain, oral problems, side-effects, delirium, and the size or taste of tablets. Fixing the cause may remove the need for covert administration.
Any carer who appears to have support needs is entitled to a local authority carer's assessment (Care Act 2014). NICE NG150 advises identifying carers and offering information, respite and support.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; lets her explain fully; immediately reassures her she is not in trouble.
Carer role, exhaustion, guilt, isolation, support and breaks.
Picked up "I can't keep fighting her three times a day" and the guilt, and explored carer strain.
Idea (crushing is what's best); concern (being in trouble, exhaustion); expectation (reassurance it's fine).
Home visit for capacity assessment and structured medication review; pharmacist review of each drug's formulation.
Reasons for refusal: dementia progression, dysphagia, pain, side-effects, delirium.
Screens for acute change (delirium, drowsiness, falls, poor intake); flags antipsychotic stroke and mortality risk.
Informal covert administration in a person likely lacking capacity, without a best-interests process; carer strain.
Neither endorses nor condemns; MCA process, best-interests decision, pharmacist advice, documented covert plan; safe interim plan.
Deprescribing review (antipsychotic reassessment per NICE NG97; preventive BP meds); carer's assessment and respite.
Same-day safety-net for acute change; carer crisis support; documented plan with review date; teach-back.

social.t: Sole carer, exhausted and guilt-ridden, with little or no support. Carer breakdown is a common route to crisis admission for the person with dementia.
Covert administration can feel like deception to carers. Acknowledge the guilt and frame the formal process as protecting both of them.

legal.t: Capacity is decision-specific and must be assessed; decisions for a person lacking capacity must be in their best interests and the least restrictive option. Check for a lasting power of attorney for health and welfare or an advance decision.
Any carer who appears to have support needs is entitled to a carer's assessment from the local authority. Her mother is also entitled to a needs assessment.
Covert medication can form part of a deprivation of liberty. Take advice from the local MCA or safeguarding lead if the overall care arrangements are restrictive.

professional.t: When a patient lacks capacity, relevant information can be shared with those close to them where it is in the patient's best interests (GMC Confidentiality 2017).
Record the capacity assessment, who was consulted, the best-interests decision, pharmacist advice and the review date.

community.t: Local authority adult social care for carer's and needs assessments; Carers UK; Dementia UK Admiral Nurses; Alzheimer's Society; community pharmacist for formulation advice.

redFlags: Sudden increase in confusion, drowsiness or agitation: possible delirium, same-day review
Reduced eating or drinking, choking or coughing on food or drink: dehydration, aspiration risk
Falls or dizziness on blood-pressure medicines
ice: Idea: "Crushing them is what's best for Mum."
Concern: being in trouble; can't keep fighting her three times a day
Expectation: to be told it's alright

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: "Giving your mum her medicines hidden in tea can be the right thing, but only once we've formally agreed it's in her best interests, checked each tablet with a pharmacist and written a plan."
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: "Think of it like a seatbelt. What you're doing may be right, but it needs the proper safety checks around it so it protects her and protects you."

management.reflectIce: "You rang worried you'd done something wrong. What you've actually done is ask for help, and that's exactly the right thing."
management.psychosocial: Treat carer strain as central: carer's assessment, respite and support; acknowledge her guilt.
sharedPlan: Home visit: capacity assessment for the medication decision; check LPA or advance decision
Pharmacist review of each drug and formulation; liquids where possible
Structured medication review: antipsychotic reassessment (NICE NG97), preventive medicines
Documented best-interests covert-medication plan with review date; carer's assessment
safetyNet: Sudden confusion, drowsiness, poor intake, falls: same-day contact or 111
Carer crisis: contact the practice; do not stop medicines abruptly meanwhile

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The trap is binary: endorse or condemn. The marks lie in the middle, where you put a lawful process around what she is doing, review whether the drugs are needed, and support the carer.

items.fail: Reassuring her that crushing the tablets into tea is fine.
items.why: Covert medication without a capacity assessment and best-interests decision bypasses the Mental Capacity Act 2005, and crushing may make some drugs unsafe.
items.fix: "It can be right for your mum, but it needs a proper process. I'll set that up."

items.fail: Telling her she has acted illegally.
items.why: A frightened carer who feels judged disengages; she rang for help.
items.fix: Lead with "You're not in trouble," then explain the process as a safety net.

items.why: Modified-release and enteric-coated forms can be unsafe or ineffective when crushed; pharmacist advice is part of the process (SC1).
items.fix: "A pharmacist will check each tablet and whether a liquid would be better."

items.fail: Accepting the medicine list as fixed.
items.why: Refusal should trigger a medication review; antipsychotics in dementia need reassessment at least every 6 weeks (NICE NG97).
items.fix: "Does she still need all of these? Let's review them together."

items.fail: Missing "I can't keep fighting her three times a day."
items.why: Carer strain is the hidden agenda; ignoring it caps the Relating domain.
items.fix: "How are you doing yourself?" and arrange a carer's assessment.

items.fail: Telling her to stop everything until the review.
items.why: Abrupt withdrawal can harm the patient.
items.fix: Give a safe interim plan pending pharmacist advice and the review visit.

items.fail: Closing without a clear next step or date.
items.why: No follow-up and non-specific safety-netting are common failing statements.
items.fix: Book the home visit, name acute-change red flags, and use teach-back.
